about: One line per work on why it is relevant, written after reading the work's full text (for books, the chapters listed under 'read'). Used by paper_list.py.

why.adegbesan2009-ec3cd9: Model of resource markets: firms can gain without luck or foresight when a resource fits them better; luck appears only as the standard alternative.
why.alvarez2007-c77d51: Contrasts discovery theory (opportunities exist, found by search and planning) with creation theory (opportunities made through action under uncertainty); frames planned versus emergent founding.
why.andel1994-c1365e: Defines serendipity as the unsought finding and lists seventeen patterns, such as successful error; notes it is often hidden when stories are told as planned.
why.andriani2018-084503: Measures exaptation in 83 new drugs: about 42 percent of new uses were exaptive, and nearly all radical ones. Links unplanned new functions to serendipity.
why.austin2012-0c5916: Twenty-case study of makers: those who can try things cheaply stay open to accidents and even court them; serendipity can be arranged.
why.baker2003-8b6743: Interview study of young firms: most were founded by improvising on a seed deal from a contact, with no prior plan; evidence of unplanned founding.
why.baker2005-a11a8f: Field study of 29 resource-poor firms defines bricolage, making do with what is at hand; founders turned discarded inputs into new offerings without a plan.
why.balzano2022-f16721: Reviews 85 management papers on serendipity, grouping them into concepts, enabling conditions, foreign market entry, and networks; treats serendipity as a capability, distinct from luck.
why.barney1986-1876f5: Argues above-normal returns come from better expectations of a resource's future value or from luck; background on luck versus foresight in firm performance.
why.bhave1994-e578fb: Interviews on 27 ventures: opportunity recognition either follows a decision to start or arises from solving a personal need; customer feedback reshapes the concept.
why.brown2005-1bf985: Short commentary arguing chance plays a large part in business success that marketing theory ignores; cites the prepared-mind idea and many lucky-break examples.
why.brownell2024-a83b1a: Analysis of 70 founder podcast interviews showing founders describe luck as a mix of favorable circumstances, noticing opportunities and acting on them, not pure chance.
why.busch2020-10a2b8: Kenyan incubator case showing how flexible space, events and leadership create conditions for chance encounters founders turn into opportunities; defines serendipity as accident plus sagacity.
why.busch2023-0bee54: Systematic review defining serendipity by agency, surprise and value, separating it from luck and targeted innovation, and modelling trigger, association and materialization.
why.busch2023-8da56d: Review defining serendipity as a valuable surprise from acting on unplanned events; gives three types and a trigger-to-enactment process, set against planning and luck.
why.carayannis2011-81b76b: Agent-based simulation of regional venture formation treats serendipity as taking in found knowledge; it works best in knowledge-rich regions. Simulated, not founder evidence.
why.cattani2005-691ffb: Fiber optics patents: knowledge built without foreseeing its later use raised performance, but only for firms that reused it. Frames luck versus foresight.
why.clough2019-7defac: Review of 150 studies on how founders search for and obtain resources; background on networks and bricolage, mentioning chance ties only in passing.
why.cohen1972-f377b5: Simulation of organizations where choices, problems and solutions meet by timing, not plan; background for solutions finding problems rather than goal-driven search.
why.cohen1990-c6e4e8: Argues that recognizing and using outside information depends on prior related knowledge, and diverse backgrounds help form novel links; a mechanism for noticing unexpected cues.
why.copeland2023-f96149: Edited volume founding serendipity science: serendipity as chance plus sagacity, distinct from luck; its entrepreneurship chapter gives a trigger-to-enactment process and three types.
why.cunha2010-5a18d7: Conceptual paper defining serendipity in organizations as an unsought finding made through analogy, distinct from bricolage and improvisation, shaped by networks and preparedness.
why.cunha2015-c88a52: Reanalyses Honda's US entry: serendipity combines preparation and openness to novelty, joined by productive doubt. Defines serendipity and links prior competence to acting on surprises.
why.daniels2019-9c36de: Survey data from 85 countries on whether success is put down to luck or hard work; background on how people credit luck.
why.davidsson2015-c4ba86: Reviews 210 papers, finds 'opportunity' too vague, and proposes external enablers, new venture ideas and opportunity confidence. Background on defining what founders act on.
why.davis2009-c3861d: Simulation of structure in changing markets: simple rules suit unpredictable opportunities, and ambiguous new markets act like games of luck. Background on planning versus improvising.
why.denrell2001-fba1d1: Simulations show learning drops options that look bad early, so risky and new options go untried; background on why unexpected paths get abandoned.
why.denrell2003-27c201: Shows that learning from observed survivors undersamples failure, so risky practices look beneficial; a caution for founder success stories told only by those who succeeded.
why.denrell2004-c7c160: Shows with a random-walk model that lasting profit gaps between firms can arise from chance alone, so lasting success is weak proof of better strategy.
why.denrell2013-4b7878: Shows lasting superior performance can come from early chance events that compound, so it does not reliably signal capability; background on luck in performance.
why.denrell2015-5707ae: Argues random variation explains patterns in firm growth and performance, with early lucky breaks amplified. Background on chance and luck, not on noticing.
why.denrell2019-a55c87: Theory paper on mistaking luck for skill and ignoring regression to the mean, creating profit chances for informed strategists. Background on luck in performance.
why.derond2007-89268a: Conceptual paper: strategy emerges from choice, chance and causal background together; chance can open options but is meaningful only against prior knowledge, shown through Viagra.
why.derond2014-e6da07: Defines serendipity as spotting meaningful pairs of events, a capability and not luck; four science cases give a typology of true and pseudo serendipity.
why.dew2009-37796f: Defines entrepreneurial serendipity as search leading to unintended discovery, combining search, chance and prior knowledge, and separates it from pure luck and spontaneous recognition.
why.eagle2004-75d973: Describes a phone app that detects nearby colleagues and prompts introductions; treats chance workplace encounters as something technology can engineer, not evidence from founders.
why.eisenhardt2001-3eb21b: Argues that in fast-moving markets firms win by seizing fleeting, unplanned opportunities within a few simple rules and backing early moves that gain traction.
why.engel2017-29f9c4: Under uncertainty, founders network without fixed goals; effectual networking creates unexpected contingencies and serendipitous new venture goals, in contrast to goal-directed networking.
why.felin2021-6b1db3: Argues firms find overlooked resources by searching with a defined need in mind; much apparent luck is prepared search. Contrasts luck with targeted search.
why.fultz2021-39e22e: Survey of 326 startups: improvisation relates to serendipity (unexpected discovery through purposeful action), more under tight resources; serendipity aids performance only in informal firms.
why.fultz2025-202492: Survey of 156 new firms: doing one task at a time goes with more unsought discoveries, which raise innovation, mainly in fast-changing industries.
why.garud2003-926111: Danish versus US wind turbines: ventures advance through many actors improvising and learning step by step, not planned breakthroughs; contrasts bricolage with targeted plans.
why.garud2011-65d6ed: Case study of 3M showing practices that let employees act on serendipitous moments and keep ideas alive; evidence on organizing for serendipity inside a firm.
why.garud2013-572ab7: Review of innovation as invention, development and implementation; notes chance starts, shifting plans and shelved ideas gaining value later. Background on unplanned venture paths.
why.garud2014-a2d9b1: Argues entrepreneurs' early projective stories set expectations that ventures often miss, costing legitimacy; ventures then revise their story and direction, as Odeo became Twitter.
why.garud2018-c63015: Argues new uses for existing discoveries emerge unexpectedly, as with 3M's Post-it notes, and proposes arrangements that raise the odds of such serendipity.
why.giustiniano2016-0b0ee9: Introduces zemblanity, self-made misfortune, as the opposite of serendipity using the Costa Concordia sinking; serendipity needs preparation, openness and doubt. Not about founders.
why.graebner2004-87c1a8: Case study of eight technology acquisitions separating expected value from serendipitous value, unplanned gains such as new markets and directions found by acquired leaders.
why.granovetter1973-32994d: Shows weak ties bridge social groups and carry new information, such as job leads, which supports the network and chance-meeting route to opportunities.
why.grimes2018-91eafb: Field study of 59 founders showing how outside feedback leads them to revise or defend ideas depending on attachment; evidence on pivots and direction changes.
why.hargadon1997-2239c7: Ethnography of a design firm showing new products arise from carrying known solutions between industries by analogy; a mechanism for ideas and remarks becoming products.
why.hargadon2001-d911f5: Historical case of Edison's electric light, won by designing it to resemble gas lighting while staying flexible. About planned fit with institutions; no chance event.
why.hargadon2006-dcbd9d: Field study of design and consulting firms: creative insights often arise in brief exchanges that join people's past experience; a mechanism for passing remarks.
why.harmeling2013-ddb167: Two founders' programs began from a mugging and a war; they treated such chance events as resources, and the paper classifies founders' responses.
why.harvey2022-610e98: Finance methods paper reconciling two bootstrap tests of whether mutual funds beat the market by skill rather than luck. Background on separating luck from skill.
why.kirtley2023-e70eaa: Seven cleantech startups: strategy changes follow new information, often unplanned opportunities, and a pivot builds from small steps, usually named only in hindsight.
why.kirzner1997-178322: Austrian account of entrepreneurial discovery as alert, surprised noticing of overlooked profit, distinct from deliberate search and pure luck. Core definition of discovery.
why.klyver2025-7a51e3: Interviews with 31 Nairobi founders show they form ties with strangers, by plan or chance meeting; chance-initiated ties often turned into useful contacts.
why.korteweg2017-f6bd22: Separates lasting skill from luck in private equity and venture capital funds; venture returns are mostly luck. Background on luck, not about founders.
why.krumboltz1998-d53ff4: Argues unplanned events are everyday and serendipity needs action to create, notice and use them; a contrast between luck and action.
why.lane2020-d1934e: Field experiment on engineered chance encounters among 15,817 scientist pairs; they yield collaboration mainly when partners share some knowledge. Setting is science, not founders.
why.liu2016-734969: Review of luck in management research in six perspectives; the serendipity section ties luck to noticing and combining chance events, with types.
why.liu2024-c28da6: Chance-model theory of luck showing high performance can reflect luck rather than merit, illustrated with citations. Background on mistaking luck for skill in success stories.
why.ma2002-d85f40: Proposes four types of business luck (pure, prepared, useful weeds, skunk work), separating passive chance from proactive preparation; firm-level, with some founder examples.
why.march1991-2654b9: Models the trade-off between exploring new options and exploiting known ones, showing learning favors exploitation; background on why planned, efficient firms may miss unexpected discoveries.
why.mcfarlane2016-385256: Interviews with 21 Glasgow music entrepreneurs: chance encounters shaped ventures, serendipity bridges planned and effectual logic, and prior knowledge lets founders exploit chance events.
why.mcmullen2006-78cdcc: Model of entrepreneurial action: prior knowledge drives attention to a possible opportunity, then motivation and doubt drive the decision to act. Covers discovery without search.
why.merton2004-2c6f10: History of the word serendipity, accident plus sagacity, our Walpole definition; shows discoveries retold to credit skill or luck, and settings that breed it.
why.merton2004-746323: Only the book's select-references list was available; it catalogues serendipity literature in science and gives no argument to summarise.
why.meyer2002-3a4528: Interviews with 20 small Danish firms found most entered Eastern Europe through chance contacts such as trade fairs or partners' offers, then built strategy afterwards.
why.mintzberg1985-9d4ec0: Case history of the National Film Board of Canada showing strategies often form without a plan, from small precedents; planned strategy is partly retrospective.
why.mintzberg1985-df70c8: Distinguishes deliberate strategy, realized as intended, from emergent strategy, patterns formed without intention; emergent patterns often lead managers to change plans.
why.mintzberg1996-8f4eed: Debate over Honda's US motorcycle entry: executives describe surprise and learning rather than a plan; a case of emergent strategy set against a planned account.
why.mirvahedi2017-ff1fb5: Twenty fast-growth firms in New Zealand and Iran: most had significant serendipity, mainly through networks and early in founding. Adds 'entrepreneurial serendipity', seeking any opportunity.
why.murayama2015-fe84e7: Survey of scientists in Japan and the US: unplanned findings go with higher-cited papers, and leaders who also manage allow plan changes. Scientists, not founders.
why.nair2020-d1b976: Conceptual model of early venture creation as emergent: ideas combine through chance and purposeful encounters, so support should add openness and connections, not pick winners.
why.nguyen2024-21848b: Encyclopedia summary of a framework from setting the stage to noticing, evaluating and acting on unexpected information. Gives a process model; no new evidence.
why.oo2025-0f6dbd: Defines serendipitous invention as an unexpected find from purposeful problem solving (Mertonian or Walpolian); among 168 Kickstarter campaigns, accident stories raised perceived innovativeness and funding.
why.otto2024-a961ad: Drug discovery interviews and observation: scientists treat anomalous data as an opening, and unexpected findings become new projects when assumptions are questioned and plans reframed.
why.pease2013-ef46e2: Splits serendipitous discovery into prepared mind, trigger, bridge and result, rated on chance, sagacity and value; builds on Merton and Barber.
why.plowman2007-c30eea: Church case: an unplanned breakfast for homeless people grew, through resources, language and symbols, into unintended radical change. Shows amplifying a small start.
why.reijonen2023-36e677: Three immigrant founders' accounts show chance meetings leading to unforeseen ventures, framed as a serendipity process enabled by small experiments, affordable loss and available resources.
why.reinsberger2025-20b5e3: Four-case study of structured expert-interview search for new uses of existing technologies; argues need-solution pairs can be found deliberately, and sets deliberate search against serendipity.
why.rosenman1988-26b8e4: Short essay on serendipity in science: Walpole's original meaning requires sagacity, penicillin shows chance meeting a prepared mind, and scientists often retell discoveries as planned.
why.ross2024-d776e3: Defines serendipity as accident plus the skill to use it, separates it from luck, and offers types and mechanisms; not about founders.
why.rumelt1991-ce1e13: Profit variance analysis: industry explains little, stable business-unit differences explain far more. Background on firm-level performance variation, not about serendipity directly.
why.sarasvathy2001-f6e40d: Contrasts causation from a fixed goal with effectuation from available means, where founders exploit contingencies and goals emerge; gives the planned versus unplanned founding contrast.
why.sarasvathy2008-b3d5c9: Book on effectuation: expert founders start from who they are, what they know and whom they know, and use surprises; contrasts planned, goal-first action.
why.shah2007-30af0c: Most juvenile-product firms were founded by users who built a solution for their own need, then saw demand from others; a route to accidental founding.
why.shane2000-cc1be0: Eight cases around one MIT invention show founders recognized only opportunities tied to their prior knowledge, without searching; prior knowledge shapes what gets noticed.
why.smith2025-07dc7b: Five-year real-time pharma consortium case: serendipity unfolds through deep-diving, listening in, connecting and implementing; one discovery matured, another died unacted on.
why.sotosimeone2021-aac9bc: Debate response arguing venture survival is not a gamble: skill, experience and founder psychology matter. Background on the skill-versus-luck dispute, not serendipity.
why.terveen2025-8db027: Six-month study of nine early founders: chance encounters that feel right bring committed action; ones that feel off prompt reframing. Evidence on acting, missed encounters.
why.trott2024-e8e576: Conceptual paper: serendipity in product development is an unexpected event, noticing, then novel association; five families of cognitive bias block each step.
why.vanlent2023-afed1a: Founding stories told afterward look planned and omit unintended, serendipitous steps; proposes historical sources to recover them. A caution for interview-based data.
why.vogel2017-d8e6ae: Separates a venture idea from a venture opportunity and names intentional generation, accidental discovery and received ideas as routes to an idea.
why.vonhippel2016-a67f44: Proposes that a need and its solution are often found together, sometimes by serendipity, with no prior problem statement, as with the rolling suitcase.
why.wareham2022-c310ad: Studies 170 funded big-science projects; serendipity is cultivated by combining technologies, moving them across fields, or using machine learning. Types and antecedents; scientists, not founders.
why.williams2015-dc48b1: Review of how entrepreneurs judge whether an opportunity suits them, using rule-based reasoning; background on opportunity evaluation, with nothing on chance or serendipity.
why.yaqub2018-fd9c19: Builds a taxonomy from 118 discovery stories: four types by search target and outcome (Walpolian, Mertonian, Bushian, Stephanian) and four mechanisms, including errors and networks.
